projects.goal: Remove forced uncertainty wrappers and generic dry responses for conversational intent without weakening execution safety.

projects.goal: No long idle periods after a blocked task becomes executable again.

success_criteria: blocked task resumes after recovery without human input
no extended idle state after readiness becomes valid
retry happens automatically and safely

Patch recovery path so stale/invalid -> valid triggers one bounded requeue attempt for the blocked task.
Prevent infinite retry loops with retry metadata and cooldown.

projects.goal: Repeated non-progressing actions trigger escalation to corrective branches.

success_criteria: repeated status-check loops are detected
branch selection changes automatically
stale repeated actions are not treated as success
tasks: Identify current action classes and repeated status-check patterns.
Classify repeated unchanged status/warning/ack responses as stale_repeated_action.
Penalize stale action classes in branch selection.
Add tests proving repeated status checks no longer persist beyond threshold.

projects.goal: MIM must not stop at problem found or objective created. It must dispatch corrective implementation work.
projects.objective: Bind detected stale or structural problems to actual implementation dispatch.
success_criteria: corrective problem detection results in actual dispatch
objective cannot complete from planning alone
result reporting shows real execution lifecycle
tasks: Reuse known stale-loop remediation targets such as gateway.py and autonomy_driver_service.py where appropriate.

Prevent objective completion without dispatch/execution attempt.

stewardship map exists

projects.goal: Runtime failures should be detectable and bounded recovery should happen automatically where safe.

tasks: Validate current health endpoints and add missing checks.

chat remains clean and usable

Create GitHub issue for staff review Abstract For real-life applications, it is crucial that end-to-end spoken language translation models perform well on continuous audio, without relying on human-supplied segmentation. For online spoken language translation, where models need to start translating before the full utterance is spoken,most previous work has ignored the segmentation problem. In this paper, we compare various methods for improving models’ robustness towards segmentation errors and different segmentation strategies in both offline and online settings and report results on translation quality, flicker and delay. Our findings on five different language pairs show that a simple fixed-window audio segmentation can perform surprisingly well given the right conditions. Donate > cs > arXiv:2210.13363 Help | Advanced Search All fields Title Author Abstract Comments Journal reference ACM classification MSC classification Report number arXiv identifier DOI ORCID arXiv author ID Help pages Full text Search GO quick links Login Help Pages About --> Computer Science > Computation and Language arXiv:2210.13363 (cs) [Submitted on 24 Oct 2022] Title: Don't Discard Fixed-Window Audio Segmentation in Speech-to-Text Translation Authors: Chantal Amrhein , Barry Haddow View a PDF of the paper titled Don't Discard Fixed-Window Audio Segmentation in Speech-to-Text Translation, by Chantal Amrhein and Barry Haddow View PDF Abstract: For real-life applications, it is crucial that end-to-end spoken language translation models perform well on continuous audio, without relying on human-supplied segmentation. For online spoken language translation, where models need to start translating before the full utterance is spoken, most previous work has ignored the segmentation problem. In this paper, we compare various methods for improving models' robustness towards segmentation errors and different segmentation strategies in both offline and online settings and report results on translation quality, flicker and delay. Our findings on five different language pairs show that a simple fixed-window audio segmentation can perform surprisingly well given the right conditions.
